query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

cited_evidence.text: Complex multi-element alloys are gaining prominence for structural applications, supplementing steels, and superalloys. Understanding the impact of each element on alloy surfaces due to oxidation is vital in maintaining material integrity. This study investigates oxidation mechanisms in these alloys using a model five-element equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy, in a controlled oxygen environment. The oxidation-induced surface changes correlate with each element’s interactive tendencies with the environment, guided by thermodynamics. Initial oxidation stages follow atomic size and redox potential, with the latter becoming dominant over time, causing composition inversion. The study employs in-situ atom probe tomography, transmission electron microscopy, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to elucidate the oxidation process and surface oxide structure evolution. Our findings deconvolute the mechanism for compositional and structural changes in the oxide film and will pave the way for a predictive design of complex alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions. Under oxidizing environments and elevated temperatures, surface speciation is highly dictated by each element’s reactivity towards the diffusing oxygen atoms (oxidation potential), albeit perturbed by their interaction with nearest neighbor atoms. Properties such as standard reduction potential (E0), cohesive energy density (CED),, and atomic radius aid in delineating the propensity and feasibility of the oxidation reaction. Thermodynamically, elements with the closest and deepest local minima act spontaneously given favorable conditions. A mechanistic understanding of these parameters creates a pathway toward designing robust alloys with superior bulk and surface properties. Ex situ observations, conducted using TEM after 120 min of oxidation, revealed a layered oxide structure. The 20 nm oxide layer on the equiatomic base alloy exhibited a composition sequence of Ni-rich (bottom layer), Cr-rich, and then Fe, Mn, and Co-rich layers (outer oxide). decision.trend: Research on multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles has been focused on understanding their synthesis-structure-property relationships, with a particular emphasis on their potential applications in catalytic and thermoelectric fields. Various physical and chemical fabrication approaches have been used to produce these nanoparticles, but their synthesis-structure-property relationships remain poorly established. Recent studies have explored the use of high-entropy alloys, atomistic simulations, and machine learning to predict and design these nanoparticles with tailored properties. Additionally, research has been conducted on the oxidation mechanisms and surface changes in these alloys, which is crucial for maintaining material integrity.

decision.why: To further understand the synthesis-structure-property relationships of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, in-situ TEM and APT can be used to characterize the nanoparticles' structure, composition, and oxidation mechanisms in real-time, providing valuable insights into their behavior under various service regimes. This approach can help identify the key factors governing the preservation of structural and chemical stability, ultimately informing the design of nanoparticles with improved performance and stability for catalytic and thermoelectric applications.
